name: Eleusine

project_scope.warning: E. indica is introduced in North America; this genus card is NOT a native-plant recommendation. Other Eleusine are outside currently installed canonical species.

look_here_first: GOOSEGRASS (INTRODUCED): go BASE → COLLAR → HEAD. (1) Annual fibrous-rooted rosette of very FLATTENED pale or silvery-white basal tillers; outward shoots come from one crown and do NOT form rooting stolons/rhizomes. (2) Young blades are FOLDED, not rolled; at the leaf-sheath junction examine a SHORT jagged, sometimes centrally notched MEMBRANOUS ligule (~0.2–1.5 mm depending on source), with hairs nearby but NOT a ligule made only of hairs. (3) A seedhead has several stiff FINGERLIKE branches, often one lower branch; each flat branch bears TWO neat zipperlike rows of flat AWNLESS spikelets. Mature spikelets about 3–7 mm and usually 3–9 fertile florets EACH; count florets inside ONE spikelet, not the seeds or branches. Only an original seedhead image was locally installed before this pass; new licensed Commons parts photographs are EXTERNAL references.

New leaf FOLDED in bud; no extensive rooting runner network

Flattened radiating branches with neat two rows of awnless spikelets

comparison_lesson.title: Goosegrass: white flat crown, membrane ligule, zipper seedhead
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: G = GOOSEGRASS: FLAT WHITE CROWN → FOLDED new LEAF → tiny notched MEMBRANE → flat zipper spikelet ROWS → 3–9 FLORETS in ONE spikelet. Cynodon has true rooted runners and a HAIR ligule; Chloris has bristly AWNED florets.
quick_split: CRABGRASS / Digitaria ciliaris: often digitate narrow head too, but spikelets are paired or arranged less rigidly along finer axes, each normally with a fertile upper and sterile lower floret; it lacks the characteristic chunky pale flattened goosegrass center. Many crabgrasses have a ROLLED young leaf where goosegrass has FOLDED vernation, but confirm the actual species before relying on this. BERMUDAGRASS / Cynodon dactylon: a PERENNIAL with true soil-running stolons that root at nodes and underground rhizomes; very short HAIR-FRINGED ligule; one-floret spikelets rather than the many-floreted goosegrass spikelet. FEATHER FINGERGRASS / Chloris virgata: fingers look hairy/FEATHERY from conspicuously LONG awns and lemma-tip hairs; goosegrass spikes are smooth-coarse and awnless in tidy flat two-row zipper units. CROWFOOTGRASS / Dactyloctenium aegyptium: compact broad spike-fingers are often short or claw-shaped, sometimes with projected point on the end; use spikelet glume/awn key. Do NOT judge from a top-down crown-like seedhead image alone.
comparison_lesson.caution: Cynodon/Digitaria/Chloris/Eleusine all may carry radial seedheads; inspect actual crown, collar, and spikelets. Preserve existing introduced/native metrics classification.

comparison_matrix.title: Finger-seedhead grasses: separate by base + ligule + one spikelet
rows: Eleusine indica — goosegrass
INTRODUCED annual; flattened pale crown, FOLDED bud, no rooted runners
Short jagged MEMBRANE ~0.2–1.5 mm
Stout flat two-row 'zipper' branches; compressed 3–7 mm spikelets with ~3–9 florets, AWNLESS
Digitaria ciliaris — southern crabgrass
Often spreading annual; finer seedhead, many species rolled bud, check same rooted specimen
Membranous, often taller/less notched
Small paired/more delicate two-floret-unit spikelets, not stout Eleusine multi-floret zippers
Cynodon dactylon — bermudagrass
Perennial rhizomes and rooting aboveground stolons
VERY SHORT FRINGE OF HAIRS
Fine digitate seedhead, usually 1 fertile floret per spikelet
Chloris virgata — feather fingergrass
Tufted annual; fuzzy fingerlike branches, no signature flat silver crown
Membranous
Conspicuous awned and hairy florets create plumose outline
Dactyloctenium aegyptium — crowfootgrass
Introduced annual tuft; short clawlike branched head
Membranous
Branches often end in bristlelike tips; glumes awned; use glume microscope

what_to_teach_crew: Nonflowering grass ID begins at the CENTER, not with seedheads: flattened whitish goosegrass annual crown.
Pull open the youngest blade at the collar. Goosegrass: FOLDED blades plus a SHORT MEMBRANOUS ligule; Bermudagrass: HAIR-FRINGE ligule and rooted perennial stolons.
Don't assume all fingers carry the same spikelets. Goosegrass has two stout parallel rows of AWNLESS, MULTIFLORET units along each branch.
The Harry Rose Commons panel provides an already annotated real individual Eleusine spikelet; distinguish the two glumes from the nested lemmas/paleas and 3–9 fertile florets.
Compare Digitaria ciliaris, Cynodon dactylon, Chloris virgata by actual licensed photographic evidence with EACH clearly a different taxon.
Keep the original source CC BY-NC-SA rights hold unresolved until separate explicit website photo eligibility approval; the extra CC BY photo references are different independently credited media.
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — one physically present original true goosegrass JPEG and 2 existing seedhead arrows; three separately source-licensed CC BY external anatomy/habit photo references plus 3 locally archived actual look-alike images. Need new physical diagnostic crown/ligule/spikelet photos and original CC BY-NC-SA website permission resolution.
visual_needs: ROOTED CROWN: whole pulled annual plant including fibrous roots and strongly flattened whitish tiller bases; small scale at the central pale crown; document absence of rooted runners.
FOLDED NEW BUD: expose newly emerging blade cross-section, compare same-scale crabgrass rolled vernation.
TRUE LIGULE 10–20×: open blade/sheath junction and point to jagged/notched ~0.2–1.5 mm transparent MEMBRANE, not adjacent collar hairs; include mm ruler.
ONE FLAT FLOWER BRANCH: side and face view demonstrating two tight rows of AWNLESS closely appressed spikelets and any lower-subtending flowering branch.
ONE FULL RIPE SPIKELET 10–20×: photograph two lower glumes plus ~3–9 fertile florets in a 3–7 mm compressed spikelet with 1-mm scale. Label florets INSIDE, not whole spikelets.
CONTROL LOOKALIKES: separately image Digitaria paired spikelet, Cynodon true rooted stolon and short hair-fringe ligule, and Chloris plumose long awns.

PUBLIC SAFE PHOTO: get an actual archived exact-species CC0/CC BY/CC BY-SA collar and crown JPG; existing CC BY-NC-SA original still carries explicit public photo-rights hold and must not be silently released.

items.label: 1 · GOOSEGRASS ORIGINAL — stiff radiating branches and zipper rows
items.image_role: Original physically archived exact species photograph; previously reviewed 2 gross-structure arrows retained, not a collar or floret microscope macro.
items.caption: Actual previously inspected María Eugenia Mendiola González goosegrass photograph. Several fingerlike flowering branches radiate near one point; the nearer branch reveals closely attached spikelets. The original two arrows remain on the visibly identifiable branch and spikelet row only. No visible white crown, true collar or dissected florets in this image.
items.why_it_matters: A field seedhead can start an ID, but white flattened crown + folded leaf + membranous ligule + single multi-floret spikelet are the separating suite.
items.creator: María Eugenia Mendiola González
items.photo_status: Source image physically verified and viewed; ORIGINAL CC BY-NC-SA photo and its unresolved public-photo eligibility kept unchanged. No new annotation or permission claim.

items.label: 2 · SAME SPECIES — entire goosegrass plant and rosette
items.image_role: Separately licensed genuine goosegrass whole-plant/habit image from Wikimedia Commons; EXTERNAL photo reference, not a local file
items.caption: Harry Rose's real Eleusine indica plant1 shows an entire tufted weed plant. Begin the search for the flattened, often white/silvery central tiller bases at the soil. It is a whole-plant reference, not certified close-up proof that its particular center shows the ligule or that every shoot's nodes are visible.
items.why_it_matters: The crew should start below the flowerhead, where goosegrass differs from many other finger-seedhead turf weeds.
items.creator: Harry Rose

items.label: 3 · SAME SPECIES — true membranous goosegrass ligule
items.image_role: Separately licensed external botanically labelled true Eleusine leaf collar/ligule diagnostic photograph; not a local image
items.caption: Harry Rose's ligule2 photograph is specifically captioned as a 0.5–1 mm short membranous ligule with a rim of short hairs, often with longer side hairs. Teach the MEMBRANE at the blade/sheath junction, not the detached collar hairs. Compare bermudagrass's hair-fringe ligule. Source photo shows a collar part, not the original archived head.
items.why_it_matters: The tiny membranous/notched ligule and folded emerging blades settle many nonflowering goosegrass-versus-Bermuda questions.
items.creator: Harry Rose
items.photo_status: EXTERNAL original CC BY 2.0 Commons photo with precise source-described anatomical role and no new arrows or local stored bytes.

items.label: 4 · SAME SPECIES — pre-annotated mature spikelet
items.image_role: Already ANNOTATED source-authored CC BY 2.0 individual spikelet macro of Eleusine indica, reuse source annotations as supplied, no locally created derivative.
items.caption: Harry Rose's pre-annotated spikelet image (a crop derived from his source) explicitly names glumes, lemmas and paleas. Look for a strongly flattened roughly 3–5 mm spikelet containing MULTIPLE florets, not the one-flowered bermudagrass spikelet. Read the photo's pre-existing labels; we added no arrow positions for microscopic anatomy.
items.why_it_matters: This fills the old anatomical teaching gap: the crew can learn the rank of WHOLE RACEME → WHOLE SPIKELET → FLORETS with a real, already labelled source photograph.

items.label: 5 · CRABGRASS LOOK-ALIKE — paired/side-view spikelet
items.image_role: Existing physically inspected and stored DIFFERENT species true Digitaria ciliaris image, not goosegrass.
items.caption: This is southern CRABGRASS, not goosegrass. The genuine archived extreme close-up shows a broad individual green crabgrass spikelet, rather than Eleusine's head-level neat two ranks of repeatedly multi-flowered spikelets. One such view cannot prove the whole Digitaria panicle, and the image should NOT be called a full paired-spikelet demonstration.
items.why_it_matters: Train separate comparison of an individual spikelet from an entire branch; crabgrass and goosegrass may both have digitate inflorescences but very different spikelet construction.
items.creator: Thomas Gyselinck
items.photo_status: Original physical Digitaria macro verified visually in GitHub; image assigned different scientific_name, no new arrows.

items.label: 6 · BERMUDAGRASS LOOK-ALIKE — actual aboveground runner
items.image_role: Existing physically inspected and archived DIFFERENT species true bermudagrass stolon/leaf-bearing node image, not goosegrass.
items.caption: This is BERMUDAGRASS, not goosegrass. This real horizontal stolon carries multiple leaf-producing nodes along a creeping perennial shoot; some roots may need a better-focused node macro, so do not label any unclear roots in this photograph. Goosegrass spreads from one flattened annual crown, without a perennial stolon network.
items.why_it_matters: Separate a 'flattened, many tillers from ONE base' from a real creeping runner with repeatedly rooted nodes.
items.creator: jimmex (iNaturalist source records: no rights reserved)
items.photo_status: Existing real Cynodon CC0 JPEG visually checked directly in GitHub, reused as different-grass comparison without false root arrows.

items.label: 7 · FEATHER FINGERGRASS LOOK-ALIKE — feathery awned branches
items.image_role: Existing physically inspected and archived DIFFERENT species Chloris virgata flowering head image, not goosegrass.
items.caption: This is FEATHER FINGERGRASS, not goosegrass. Its radiating or gathered branches look plumose and bristly from lemma awns/hairs, whereas goosegrass has fairly regular, stout, toothlike AWNLESS spikelet rows in a zipper pattern. This gross photo cannot measure exact awn length of any one fertile lemma.
items.why_it_matters: Both produce crowfoot-like heads; inspect the individual spikelets for awns rather than relying on branch count.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Existing actual Matt Lavin CC BY-SA 2.0 Chloris image individually inspected in GitHub, different species comparison only.
